prompt: Why are radical addition reactions of limited use on complex molecules in the laboratory?

choices.text: The radical intermediate isn't quenched and reacts again and again uncontrollably
Radicals are too unreactive to add to carbon–carbon double bonds
choices.why: The problem is the opposite: radicals are highly reactive.

choices.text: A nucleophile quenches the radical intermediate after just one addition
choices.why: That describes the cation in an electrophilic addition, which is why those reactions are controllable.

choices.text: Radical additions can only be started inside an enzyme's active site
choices.why: Laboratory radical reactions start with initiators such as benzoyl peroxide; the difficulty is control.

explanation: The high reactivity of radicals makes controlled reactions difficult. In electrophilic addition the reaction occurs once and the cation is rapidly quenched by a nucleophile. A radical intermediate is not usually quenched; it reacts again and again in a largely uncontrollable way.

prompt: In an electrophilic addition to an alkene, what usually happens to the reactive cation intermediate?

choices.text: It is rapidly quenched by a nucleophile after a single addition
It adds to another alkene molecule, starting a chain of additions
choices.why: Chain-building repeated additions are typical of radical intermediates.

choices.text: It survives and goes on reacting again and again uncontrollably
It gains an electron from the alkene and becomes a radical
choices.why: The cation is quenched by a nucleophile, which completes the addition.

explanation: In electrophilic addition, reaction occurs once and the reactive cation intermediate is rapidly quenched by a nucleophile. A radical intermediate, by contrast, usually isn't quenched and reacts again and again.

prompt: Why are radical reactions more controlled, and more common, in biological systems than in the laboratory?

choices.text: An enzyme holds one substrate at a time in a precise position near the reacting groups
Radicals formed in cells are much less reactive than laboratory radicals
choices.why: The control comes from the enzyme's active site, not from lower radical reactivity.

choices.text: Enzymes quench every radical with a nucleophile immediately after it forms
choices.why: In prostaglandin biosynthesis the radicals go on to several further additions; control comes from precise positioning.

choices.text: Cells run radical reactions at very high temperatures and pressures
choices.why: High temperature and pressure were used for industrial ethylene polymerization, not in cells.

explanation: In an enzyme's active site, only one substrate molecule is present at a time, held in a precise position with the other necessary reacting groups nearby. As a result, biological radical reactions are more controlled and more common than laboratory or industrial ones.

prompt: How many radical additions take place in the biosynthesis of prostaglandins from arachidonic acid?
explanation: A sequence of four radical additions takes place: steps 2 and 5 are radical additions to O2, and steps 3 and 4 are radical additions to carbon–carbon double bonds. The entire process is catalyzed by a single enzyme.

prompt: How does prostaglandin biosynthesis from arachidonic acid begin?

choices.text: An iron–oxy radical abstracts a hydrogen atom from carbon 13
O2 adds to the double bond between carbons 8 and 9
choices.why: O2 adds later; the first step is hydrogen abstraction at carbon 13.

choices.text: A proton adds to a double bond to give a carbocation
choices.why: The pathway is radical, not polar: it starts with hydrogen-atom abstraction.

choices.text: An iron–oxy radical adds to the double bond between carbons 12 and 13
choices.why: The iron–oxy radical removes an H atom from carbon 13; it doesn't add to a double bond.

explanation: The pathway begins with abstraction of a hydrogen atom from carbon 13 of arachidonic acid by an iron–oxy radical, giving a carbon radical. Through a resonance form, that radical reacts with O2 at carbon 11.

prompt: In prostaglandin biosynthesis, the carbon radical formed by removing H from carbon 13 reacts with O2 through a resonance form. At which carbon (give its number) does this first O2 bond?
explanation: The carbon radical formed by hydrogen abstraction at carbon 13 reacts with O2 at carbon 11 through a resonance form. The resulting oxygen radical then adds to the double bond between carbons 8 and 9.

prompt: In prostaglandin biosynthesis, what does the oxygen radical formed from the first O2 do next?

choices.text: It adds to the double bond between carbons 8 and 9, leaving a radical at carbon 8
It removes a hydrogen atom from carbon 13, leaving a radical there
choices.why: Hydrogen abstraction at carbon 13 was the first step, before any O2 added.

choices.text: It adds to the double bond between carbons 12 and 13, leaving a radical at carbon 13
choices.why: That addition is made next, by the carbon radical at carbon 8.

choices.text: It is reduced at once, breaking the O–O bond and giving PGH2
choices.why: Reduction of the O–O bond is the last step, after a second O2 has added.

explanation: The oxygen radical adds to the double bond between carbons 8 and 9 to give a carbon radical at carbon 8. That radical adds to the double bond between carbons 12 and 13, giving a radical at carbon 13.

prompt: In prostaglandin biosynthesis, a resonance form of the carbon-13 radical adds to a second O2 molecule. At which carbon (give its number) does this happen?
explanation: After the carbon-8 radical adds to the double bond between carbons 12 and 13, the new radical at carbon 13 reacts through a resonance form at carbon 15 with a second O2 molecule, completing the prostaglandin skeleton.

prompt: Once the prostaglandin skeleton is complete, what final step gives prostaglandin H2 (PGH2)?

choices.text: Reduction of the O–O bond
Addition of a third O2 molecule
choices.why: Only two O2 molecules add, at carbons 11 and 15.

choices.text: Abstraction of a hydrogen atom from carbon 13
choices.why: That is the first step of the pathway.

choices.text: Hydration of a remaining double bond
choices.why: The section says reduction of the O–O bond gives PGH2.

explanation: After the second O2 adds at carbon 15, reduction of the O–O bond gives prostaglandin H2. The whole pathway is catalyzed with exquisite control by a single enzyme.

prompt: How many O2 molecules are incorporated as arachidonic acid is converted into prostaglandin H2?
explanation: Two of the four radical additions are additions to O2: the first at carbon 11 (step 2) and the second at carbon 15 (step 5). The other two (steps 3 and 4) are additions to carbon–carbon double bonds.
